summaries.example: Imagine a school app that records when you arrive, what books you borrow, and which clubs you visit. The app may help the school organize activities, but students and families should know what is collected and why. They may also want rules that stop the information from being used for unrelated purposes.
summaries.summary: Privacy means having some control over access to information about yourself and over situations where others can learn about you. Information technology makes it easy to collect, store, search, and combine data from phones, websites, purchases, cameras, and other devices. This can be useful, but it can also allow people or organizations to harm someone, treat them unfairly, or pressure their choices. The philosophical debate asks what privacy is, why it has value, and how much control people should have. Some thinkers say privacy protects other goods, such as safety, freedom, friendship, dignity, or democracy. Others say privacy matters in its own right. A further view treats privacy as a group of related concerns rather than one single thing. Laws may require permission, limited purposes, notice, correction of errors, and accountability. Technology can help too, through encryption, anonymous communication, careful settings, and systems designed to protect privacy from the start. Still, no tool is perfect, and too many confusing choices can place an unfair burden on users.
key_ideas: Privacy is not only about hiding secrets. It can also mean having a say in who gets access to information about you.
Computers, phones, websites, and connected devices can collect and combine huge amounts of personal data.
Personal data can be misused to cause harm, treat people unfairly, or influence their choices.
People disagree about why privacy matters. Some see it as valuable in itself; others connect it to safety, freedom, dignity, friendship, or democracy.
Rules and technology can help protect data, but people cannot always understand every choice or control every use.
Privacy-friendly systems should limit data collection, explain purposes, and protect information throughout its life.
summaries.why_it_matters: Personal information can affect real opportunities and relationships. A location record might reveal where someone lives. An online profile might change which advertisements, prices, or opportunities they see. If information moves from one setting to another, it may be misunderstood or used unfairly. Learning about privacy helps people ask better questions and helps designers, companies, and governments think about their responsibilities.

important_terms.definition: Privacy is having some control over who can know things about you and when they can know them.
Personal data is information connected, or connectable, to a particular person, such as a name, location, or online activity.
Information technology means computer systems and networks that store, use, and share information.
Consent means agreeing after being given understandable information about what will happen.
Privacy by design means building privacy protections into a product from the beginning, rather than adding them only after trouble occurs.

questions_to_think_about: When should an app ask before collecting information?
Should information collected for one purpose be used for another purpose?
Is privacy still important when someone has nothing to hide?
Who should be responsible when a computer system misuses personal data?

summaries.example: Suppose a health app collects exercise, sleep, location, and search data. It uses these records to suggest habits, but the same profile could also be used by an insurer, advertiser, or employer. Even if no one reads a private diary, the profile may influence decisions about the person. A privacy-sensitive design would specify the purpose, seek meaningful permission, restrict access, reduce unnecessary collection, and provide ways to inspect or correct the data.
summaries.summary: The entry examines privacy as a philosophical, legal, and technological problem. One central distinction is between decisional privacy—the freedom to make intimate personal choices without interference—and informational privacy—the interest in controlling access to information about oneself, the circumstances that reveal it, and the technologies that process it. Privacy can be described as a social condition, or defended normatively as something that ought to be protected. Its value is disputed. Reductionist theories explain it through goods such as security, autonomy, intimacy, dignity, liberty, democracy, or economic fairness. Non-reductionist theories regard privacy as valuable in itself, while cluster theories identify several related claims without a single defining core. Other approaches emphasize knowledge, contextual appropriateness, or freedom from arbitrary data-based power. Personal data includes information explicitly supplied by a person as well as behavioral records, metadata, and information that can be inferred. Information technology expands the ability to collect, connect, store, and analyze such data through internet services, social media, mobile devices, connected objects, artificial intelligence, and surveillance systems. This creates risks of harm, unequal bargaining power, discrimination, function creep, manipulation, and chilling effects on choice. Protection may involve law, informed consent, specified purposes, limited use, correction, accountability, and oversight. Technical measures such as encryption, anonymization, attribute-based identity systems, and privacy-enhancing tools can assist, but they have limits and may be difficult to use correctly. key_ideas: The entry distinguishes decisional privacy from informational privacy: freedom in personal decisions is not the same issue as control over personal data.
Privacy claims can be descriptive, reporting how people understand privacy, or normative, arguing how information use ought to be constrained.
There is no settled agreement about privacy’s value. Major approaches connect it to other values, defend it as independently valuable, or describe a cluster of related concerns.
Information technology increases connectivity and makes large-scale storage, combination, prediction, and surveillance possible. Greater access therefore creates both benefits and risks.
Risks include harm, informational inequality, discrimination across contexts, reduced autonomy, and loss of accountability when decisions rely on opaque profiles.
Law and design can provide indirect control: purpose limitation, informed consent, access and correction, oversight, encryption, identity management, and privacy by design.
summaries.why_it_matters: Digital records can shape how people are seen and treated, even when the person never intentionally supplied the relevant conclusion. A profile may be assembled from many ordinary actions and then used in another context. Privacy matters because access to data can change power relationships, opportunities, participation in democracy, and people’s willingness to explore ideas or act freely. Understanding the competing arguments helps clarify what protections should require and who should provide them.

important_terms.definition: Informational privacy is the moral interest in controlling access to information about oneself, situations that reveal it, and technologies that generate or process it.
Decisional or constitutional privacy concerns freedom to make intimate and personal decisions without interference; it differs from control over personal information.
Personal data is information linked, or capable of being linked, to an identifiable natural person, including explicit, behavioral, and metadata information.
A reductionist account explains privacy’s value through other values, such as autonomy, security, dignity, liberty, intimacy, democracy, or economic interests.
A cluster account treats privacy as a collection of connected moral claims rather than as having one essential feature.
Profiling uses data to construct a picture of a person or group and to predict interests, traits, or behavior.
Function creep occurs when data gathered for one stated purpose is later used for different purposes.
Privacy-enhancing technology is a technical tool or method intended to reduce unwanted access to or identification through personal data.

questions_to_think_about: Does privacy have value apart from safety, autonomy, dignity, or democracy?
When does a data profile become a decision about a person rather than merely information about them?
Can consent be meaningful when refusing data collection means losing access to an important service?
Should data collected in one context normally remain within that context?
How should responsibility be divided among users, designers, companies, and governments?

summaries.example: A video-sharing app asks Maya to turn on location services. It says location will help recommend nearby videos, but the data might also be kept, combined with other activity, or shown to advertisers. Maya may want a clear choice, a setting that starts with sharing turned off, and an explanation of whether the information can be used later for something else.
summaries.summary: Privacy and information technology are closely connected because information is one way people gain access to one another. Privacy can mean having room to make personal decisions without interference, or having control over information about oneself. The first is often called decisional or constitutional privacy; the second is informational privacy. The entry explains that people disagree about the value of privacy. Some theories reduce its importance to other values, such as security, autonomy, dignity, liberty, intimacy, democracy, or economic fairness. Other theories defend privacy as independently valuable, while cluster theories see several connected concerns rather than one simple definition. Personal data includes obvious details such as a name or location, but also browsing behavior, device records, and information inferred from patterns. Internet services, social media, mobile phones, connected household devices, artificial intelligence, and government or commercial surveillance make it possible to gather and combine data on a large scale. This can bring convenience and useful services, but it can also cause harm, unequal treatment, discrimination, manipulation, or a loss of freedom when people act differently because they feel watched. Data protection aims to give people safeguards such as informed permission, a stated purpose, limited use, notice, correction, and accountability. Technical methods—including encryption, anonymous communication, identity systems, and privacy-friendly design—can support these aims. Yet tools may fail, be difficult to configure, or leave too many decisions to users. The broader lesson is that privacy depends on people, technology, organizations, and law working together.
key_ideas: Privacy includes different questions: freedom to make personal decisions and control over information are related but not identical.
Philosophers disagree about whether privacy is valuable by itself or because it protects other things, such as safety, freedom, dignity, relationships, or democracy.
Data can be collected directly, observed through behavior, or inferred by combining records. A person may not know what a system can conclude.
Technology can make sharing easy and useful while also making it hard to understand who receives information and how long it remains available.
Using information outside its original setting can create unfairness. A fact shared with a doctor may have a different meaning when used by a seller or insurer.
Privacy rules and tools can help, but consent screens, privacy settings, and anonymization do not automatically solve every problem.
summaries.why_it_matters: Information about a person can travel far beyond the moment when it was collected. It can be combined with other records and used to make judgments that are hard to see or challenge. Privacy protections can reduce opportunities for harm and unfair treatment, preserve people’s freedom to think and participate, and make organizations answerable for how they use data. The issue affects everyday choices as well as wider questions about power and democracy.

important_terms.definition: Privacy is a person’s ability to control, or place limits on, access to personal information and personal life.
Informational privacy focuses on who can obtain, use, or share information about a person.
Decisional privacy concerns being free to make intimate personal choices without outside interference.
Personal data is information linked or linkable to an individual, including online actions, location, device details, and inferred traits.
Profiling is building a picture of a person from data in order to predict interests, behavior, or group membership.
Informational inequality occurs when organizations know much more about data practices and have more power to negotiate than individuals do.
Privacy by design means making privacy a requirement during planning, building, use, and disposal of a system.
Encryption changes information into a protected form so that only an authorized party can read it, when the system is used properly.

questions_to_think_about: Is clicking “agree” enough to count as informed consent?
Should a company be allowed to predict a trait that a person never directly shared?
Why might information be acceptable in one context but unfair in another?
Can stronger privacy settings reduce the usefulness of a social network?
Who should check whether a powerful surveillance system is being used fairly?
